name: Carême and edible architecture
strand: The people who invented modern cuisine
scope: Marie-Antoine Carême (1784-1833), 'the king of chefs and the chef of kings' who cooked for Talleyrand, the future George IV and Tsar Alexander I, built dining centerpieces you could actually eat. T1: a piece montee was a towering table CENTERPIECE built entirely from food -- spun sugar, marzipan and pastry -- not flowers or metal. T2: Careme modeled these edible towers on real BUILDINGS he copied from library prints -- Greek temples, Egyptian pyramids, Chinese pagodas -- rebuilt in sugar and nougat. T3: trained partly in architecture, he declared PASTRY the highest branch of it ('the fine arts are five... whereof the principal branch is confectionery'). T4: he is credited with perfecting the VOL-AU-VENT, a tall hollow ultra-light PUFF-PASTRY case ('flying on the wind') you fill with a creamy ragout. T5: the CROQUEMBOUCHE -- a cone-shaped TOWER of cream-filled choux puffs glued with spun caramel, still the French celebration centerpiece -- is his edible architecture in its purest form.
source: Grokipedia pages 'Marie-Antoine Carême', 'Pièce montée', 'Croquembouche' (surfaced in search; direct fetch 403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Pièce montée' & 'Croquembouche', escoffier.edu chef-uniform history, thefrenchlife/cookerdiary profiles
framing_note: Wonder/prep voice: lead with the SCENE (a tower on the table you can eat), never 'Who was Careme?'. Every answer is food-anchored -- the sugar-and-pastry centerpiece, the puff-pastry vol-au-vent, the caramel-glued croquembouche, the confectionery-is-architecture claim -- the patrons and the 'king of chefs' title are HOOK/context only, never the tested answer. Accuracy rail: pieces montees were sugar/marzipan/pastry (pate d'office, nougat, spun sugar), NOT inedible props; vol-au-vent and croquembouche are genuinely credited to/perfected by Careme. Sauces are OWNED by the mother-sauce ladder -- this ladder stays on edible architecture + pastry to avoid overlap. Dinner-test payoff = T2, the edible pyramids and temples copied from architecture prints.

name: Escoffier and the kitchen brigade
strand: The people who invented modern cuisine
scope: Auguste Escoffier (1846-1935) turned the shouting, chaotic kitchen into a disciplined line. T2: a busy professional kitchen splits into STATIONS, each cook mastering one job, so a plate is built up as it passes down the line -- the brigade de cuisine, modeled on the ARMY units Escoffier served in. T3: stations are named for the FOOD they make -- the SAUCIER runs sauces near the top of the hierarchy, the GARDE-MANGER runs the cold station (salads, pates, charcuterie). T4: Escoffier SIMPLIFIED Careme's fussy grande cuisine into a leaner, faster 'cuisine classique' and wrote the whole system down in Le Guide Culinaire (1903), still a working chef's bible. T5a: he invented dishes named for celebrity guests -- PEACH MELBA (peaches + vanilla ice cream + raspberry) for opera star Nellie Melba, first served perched on an ice swan from her opera. T5b: when Melba wanted her toast paper-thin, he part-toasted it, split it in two, and toasted the cut sides -- MELBA TOAST. T5c: partnering with hotelier Cesar Ritz (the Savoy, then the Ritz/Carlton), he made the grand-HOTEL restaurant the temple of fine dining and banned shouting and drinking in his kitchens.
source: Wikipedia 'Peach Melba' & 'Auguste Escoffier'; classicalcalifornia.org and PBS Food (Escoffier/Melba story); escoffier.edu (brigade + Ritz)
framing_note: SCENE-LED (the line moving a plate through stations; the dessert on an ice swan). Answers are food/kitchen-anchored -- a station defined by the food it makes, a named dish, a technique -- never a bare biography date. Accuracy rail: Peach Melba = peaches + vanilla ice cream + raspberry puree (the raspberry was added later at the Ritz); it began as 'peche au cygne' on a swan. The sauce reform belongs to the mother-sauce ladder -- here keep Escoffier's contribution to the brigade + celebrity dishes + Ritz, no sauce-count overlap. Dinner-test payoff = T5a/T5b, the two dishes he named for the singer.

name: How the restaurant was born
strand: The people who invented modern cuisine
scope: The restaurant is a French invention barely 250 years old -- and the word first named a FOOD, not a place. T2: in 1760s Paris the word 'restaurant' meant a rich, RESTORATIVE MEAT BROTH sold to revive you -- a bouillon -- and the room took the food's name. T3: the new idea was the FORMAT -- your own small table plus a CHOICE from a printed list (a menu) at fixed prices -- versus the old inn's table d'hote where everyone shared one set meal at a common table. T4: the FRENCH REVOLUTION supercharged it -- when aristocrats fled or fell, their private chefs had no masters, so palace-level GRANDE CUISINE spilled out into public restaurants anyone could pay to enter. T5: the famous 'Monsieur Boulanger, 1765' origin tale -- a broth-seller supposedly sued by the caterers' guild for daring to serve SHEEP'S FEET in a white sauce -- is a colorful story historians can't actually document (label it legend).
source: Wikipedia 'Restaurant'; Britannica 'A. Boulanger'; National Geographic 'Who Invented the First Modern Restaurant'; parisfoodhistory.blogspot 'Boulanger and the restaurant: snowballing of a myth'
framing_note: Food-DRIVEN history where the FOOD is the anchor (the restorative broth; grande cuisine escaping the palace) -- never a bare law or policy. SCENE-LED / INVERT THE WONDER: 'the word restaurant first meant a food you drank.' Accuracy rail: the Boulanger 1765 sign-and-lawsuit tale is traditional legend, not documented -- frame it as 'the story goes,' credit the real spread to the later Revolution era. Dinner-test payoff = T2, that 'restaurant' first named a broth.

name: Julia Child brings France home
strand: The people who invented modern cuisine
scope: Julia Child (1912-2004) convinced ordinary Americans they could cook real French food. T1: she reached millions through one of the first-ever TV COOKING shows, 'The French Chef' (1963), teaching technique live on camera -- fumbles, dropped pans and all. T2: her breakthrough was writing French recipes with such patient, exact, tested steps that a HOME cook with a normal kitchen could actually follow them -- demystifying French cooking without dumbing it down. T3: the book was 'Mastering the Art of French Cooking' (1961), co-written with two French cooks, Simone Beck and Louisette Bertholle, after Julia trained at the Paris cooking school LE CORDON BLEU. T4: her signature teaching dish -- the one she cooked on her very first broadcast -- was BOEUF BOURGUIGNON, beef slowly braised in red wine, the recipe that made French technique feel doable at an American stove.
source: Wikipedia 'Mastering the Art of French Cooking'; WGBH/GBH (The French Chef, boeuf bourguignon); juliachildfans.com cookbook list
framing_note: Answers stay food-anchored -- the TV cooking show, the technique-made-doable idea, the braise-in-red-wine dish -- not a bare bio date. SCENE-LED (Julia at the stove on camera). Accuracy rail: co-authored with Simone Beck & Louisette Bertholle; the book came first (1961), the show followed (1963) -- keep that order straight. Dinner-test payoff = T4, boeuf bourguignon as the make-it-at-home French classic.

name: How a kitchen earns Michelin stars
strand: The people who invented modern cuisine
scope: The world's most coveted restaurant award was invented by a TIRE company. T2: the Michelin brothers published a free road guide in 1900 to get France's few drivers to DRIVE MORE, wear out their tires, and buy replacements -- restaurant listings were bait to sell rubber. T3: the STAR rating came later (single stars 1926, the full ladder 1931) and is judged only on what's on the PLATE -- not the decor or the tablecloths. T4: the tiers have precise meanings -- one star 'worth a stop,' two 'worth a detour,' three 'worth a SPECIAL JOURNEY' (cross the country just to eat there). T5: stars are awarded by ANONYMOUS inspectors who book, eat and pay like any other guest so the kitchen can't put on a show for them -- and losing a star can end a chef's career.
source: Wikipedia 'Michelin Guide'; guide.michelin.com official history; CNN Business 'Michelin Guide history'
framing_note: Food-anchored: the award is FOR the cooking on the plate -- keep answers on the food and the judging, not corporate trivia for its own sake. INVERT THE WONDER with the hook 'a tire company runs fine dining's top prize.' Accuracy rail: stars judge the food only (not service/decor, which affect the separate cutlery ranking); three stars = 'worth a special journey.' Dinner-test payoff = T2, that the guide exists to sell tires.

name: Brillat-Savarin, the first food writer
strand: The people who invented modern cuisine
scope: A French lawyer turned the pleasures of the table into a subject worth studying. T2: a famous soft, buttery French CHEESE -- a rich triple-cream -- is named Brillat-Savarin after him, even though he was a food WRITER who never made cheese (it was named in his honor a full century after his death). T3: a ring-shaped cake soaked in rum-and-sugar SYRUP, the SAVARIN (a close cousin of the baba au rhum), also carries his name. T4: his 1825 book 'The Physiology of Taste' was the first to treat eating and flavor as a serious ART worth analyzing -- the home of the line 'tell me what you eat and I'll tell you what you are.' T5: in that book he blamed getting fat on eating too much BREAD, FLOUR and SUGAR (starchy carbs) and told the overweight to cut them -- often called an ancestor of the modern low-carb idea, and presented here as HIS 1825 claim, not settled nutrition science.
source: Wikipedia 'Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin', 'Brillat-Savarin cheese' (created 1890 as 'Excelsior', renamed by the Androuët family ~1930s), 'Rum baba' / Savarin (Julien Brothers, 1844); academia.edu philosophical reading of Physiology of Taste
framing_note: Food-anchored: the answers are the cheese, the rum-soaked ring cake, and the starch-makes-you-fat claim -- the famous aphorism is HOOK/context, never the tested answer (no bare-quote rungs). Accuracy rail: the cheese was named FOR him decades after he died, not invented by him -- don't imply he made it; attribute the low-carb idea as his 1825 opinion, not a health verdict. Dinner-test payoff = T5, the 200-year-old 'starch makes you fat' claim.

name: Fannie Farmer makes recipes work
strand: The people who invented modern cuisine
scope: Before 1896, recipes said 'a lump of butter' or 'a teacup of flour' and the result was a gamble. T1: Fannie Farmer's fix was the LEVEL measurement -- scrape the cup or spoon flat with a knife so everyone measures the SAME amount every single time. T2: she put it in 'The Boston Cooking-School Cook Book' (1896), which sold in the millions and earned her the nickname 'the mother of LEVEL measurements.' T3: the real payoff is REPRODUCIBILITY -- a recipe now turns out the same in any kitchen for any cook because the amounts are exact (she called correct measuring 'absolutely necessary to insure the best results'). T4: it's why American recipes still measure by CUPS and SPOONS (by volume) while much of the world weighs ingredients on a scale -- Farmer's system stuck.
source: Boston Magazine (Boston Cooking-School Cook Book); amazingwomeninhistory 'mother of level measurements'; massmoments.org 'Fannie Farmer Cookbook Published'
framing_note: Food-anchored: the answer is the measuring TECHNIQUE and why the food comes out the same -- a cooking mechanism, not a bio fact. SCENE-LED: the vague 'lump of butter' versus the leveled spoon. Accuracy rail: she standardized and popularized LEVEL measuring in 1896 -- don't credit her with inventing the measuring cup itself. Dinner-test payoff = T1, scraping the cup level so the recipe actually works.

name: Nouvelle cuisine lightens up
strand: The people who invented modern cuisine
scope: In the 1970s French chefs rebelled against heavy, flour-thickened grande cuisine. T3: NOUVELLE CUISINE meant lighter, fresher food -- SHORTER cooking to keep vegetables crisp and bright green, and dropping the heavy flour-roux sauces (espagnole, bechamel) in favor of quick reductions with fresh herbs, good butter and lemon. T4: it moved plating off the big shared platter and onto the individual PLATE, arranged by the chef -- the birth of the small-portion, artfully composed plate diners now expect. T5: its figurehead PAUL BOCUSE created the soupe aux truffes 'V.G.E.' (1975) for the French president -- black truffle and foie gras in a rich broth, sealed under a dome of PUFF PASTRY that bakes up tall, traps every aroma, and is cracked open at the table.
source: Wikipedia 'Nouvelle cuisine'; SBS Food 'How Paul Bocuse changed French cuisine'; fr.wikipedia 'Soupe aux truffes noires VGE' (25 Feb 1975); guide.michelin.com Bocuse article; Grokipedia 'Gault Millau'
framing_note: Food-anchored: answers are the lighter/shorter technique, the plated-not-platter idea, and the puff-pastry-dome soup -- never a chef's biography. Accuracy rail: 'nouvelle cuisine' was coined by the Gault-Millau critics (~1973) to describe Bocuse's circle; the VGE soup dates to 1975. BANNED as answer: the soup's gram-by-gram recipe -- the payoff is the puff-pastry dome that seals the aroma. Dinner-test payoff = T5, cracking the pastry crust on Bocuse's truffle soup.

name: Ferran Adria reinvents the dish
strand: The people who invented modern cuisine
scope: At elBulli in Spain, chef Ferran Adria rebuilt familiar food from scratch. T2: his signature trick was SPHERIFICATION -- turning a plain liquid (olive juice, melon juice) into a soft SPHERE with a thin skin that looks solid but BURSTS in your mouth to release the flavor (the famous 'liquid olive' that isn't an olive at all). T3: he served savory FOAMS -- the pure taste of, say, beetroot or almond whipped into a light airy cloud, so a familiar flavor arrives in a totally unfamiliar form. T4: his method was DECONSTRUCTION -- take a dish everyone knows, keep its exact flavors, but rebuild its texture and shape so you don't recognize it until you taste it. T5: elBulli was voted the world's best restaurant a record number of times and served a 30-plus-course tasting menu -- then Adria CLOSED it at its peak (2011) to turn it into a food-research lab.
source: Britannica 'Ferran Adria'; molecularrecipes.com (spherification history at elBulli); theworlds50best.com '12 iconic dishes of elBulli'
framing_note: Wonder voice: INVERT with the sensory hook (an 'olive' that bursts into liquid). Food-anchored answers = the burst-in-the-mouth sphere, the flavor-as-foam, the deconstruction idea -- the CONCEPT, never lab jargon. Accuracy rail: BANNED as the tested answer are the chemistry names (sodium alginate / calcium bath) -- they may appear only as a distractor or context; Adria himself disliked the label 'molecular gastronomy.' Dinner-test payoff = T2, the liquid olive that looks solid and bursts.

name: The Catherine de' Medici myth
strand: The people who invented modern cuisine
scope: A famous story says French cooking was born the day an Italian teenager married into the French crown -- and it's mostly a MYTH. T3: the popular tale claims Catherine de' Medici (who married the French king's son in 1533) shipped in Italian cooks, the fork, and refined dishes that single-handedly 'created' French cuisine. T4: food historians (Barbara Ketcham Wheaton) show this is false -- real French haute cuisine took shape a CENTURY later with no Italian fingerprint on it, and the whole story only appears in writing in the 1800s, long after the fact. T5: the deeper truth is that great cuisines grow SLOWLY from many hands, regions and generations -- no single wedding or hero 'invents' a national kitchen (label the Medici tale as legend).
source: Wikipedia 'Catherine de' Medici' (myth section citing Barbara Ketcham Wheaton 'Savoring the Past' & Stephen Mennell); thenewgastronome & frenchly.us (myth debunk)
framing_note: Myth-buster: the accuracy rail IS the topic -- state the Medici story, then correct it and label it legend. Food-anchored: the disputed items are cooks, forks and dishes; the payoff is a true fact about how cuisines actually form. NO ANACHRONISM: never repeat the false 'she brought the fork/the tomato' claims as if true. Dinner-test payoff = T4, that historians have debunked the story everyone repeats.

name: Why chefs wear the tall white hat
strand: The people who invented modern cuisine
scope: The chef's uniform is a working tool with a story in every fold. T1: the tall pleated white hat is a TOQUE, and the legend says its roughly 100 PLEATS once bragged the 100 ways a master could cook an EGG (a fun tale, not actually proven). T2: the white DOUBLE-BREASTED jacket is double-breasted on purpose -- flip the buttoned flap over to hide a stain (and get two layers of cloth against stove heat and splashes) -- and white was chosen to prove the cook is CLEAN. T3: Careme made the toque TALL -- in his kitchen chefs wore different heights by RANK, his own the tallest at about 18 inches, stiffened with cardboard -- and Escoffier later made the whole white uniform the standard for every kitchen.
source: escoffier.edu 'A History of the Chef's Hat' & 'A Brief History of the Chef's Uniform'; ciachef.edu; Wikipedia 'Chef's uniform'; Grokipedia 'Chef's uniform'
framing_note: Wonder/prep voice. Food/kitchen-anchored: the answers are the hat, the reversible jacket, the rank-by-height -- kitchen gear, not a bare biography. Accuracy rail: '100 pleats = 100 ways to cook an egg' is unverified LEGEND -- frame it as 'the story goes,' not a fact. This mini OWNS the toque and uniform facts so they don't overlap the Careme ladder. Dinner-test payoff = T1, the 100-eggs pleat legend.

name: Alice Waters and farm-to-table
strand: The people who invented modern cuisine
scope: In 1971 an American chef built a whole restaurant around the INGREDIENTS instead of the recipes. T2: Alice Waters opened Chez Panisse in Berkeley and championed FARM-TO-TABLE -- cooking with produce grown LOCALLY and picked in SEASON, bought straight from nearby farmers, on the belief that a perfect ripe ingredient needs almost nothing done to it. T3: her menu CHANGES with whatever is ripe that week -- a single fixed daily menu set by the season's harvest, the opposite of a giant do-anything menu (the style that became known as 'California cuisine'). T4: she carried the idea into schools with the EDIBLE SCHOOLYARD (1995), where kids grow, harvest and cook their own food in a garden classroom.
source: Wikipedia 'Chez Panisse' & 'Alice Waters'; Smithsonian Magazine (Chez Panisse launched farm-to-table); CNN Travel (Alice Waters journey)
framing_note: Food-anchored: the answers are the local/seasonal-ingredient idea, the harvest-set menu, and the school garden -- never a bare bio date. SCENE-LED (a menu that changes with what's ripe). Accuracy rail: Chez Panisse opened 1971; Waters is a pioneer and popularizer of American farm-to-table, not the lone inventor of the concept. Dinner-test payoff = T2, that the ripe ingredient itself is the star of the plate.
